facts.text: Sold as "Andy Warhol's Frankenstein," but Warhol barely took part: he visited the set once and dropped by briefly during editing. Director Paul Morrissey made the film.
The idea came from director Roman Polanski, who told Paul Morrissey he'd be a natural to make a 3-D Frankenstein. Morrissey said he thought it was "the most absurd option I could imagine."
Roman Polanski tried 3-D on his own Rome-shot comedy What? (1972), decided it was useless, then offered the leftover equipment to Paul Morrissey for a couple of cheap films, including this one.
Despite the Warhol-branded marketing, only the single word "Frankenstein" appeared in the title on the actual print of the film.
All this gore reportedly cost about $450,000. It went on to earn $4.7 million in North American rentals, and the Los Angeles Times said it had grossed $7 million by 1974.
Udo Kier's German-accented Baron Frankenstein monologues are nearly impossible to follow, which The Bedlam Files suggests was at least partly director Paul Morrissey's intent.
Director Paul Morrissey persuaded producer Carlo Ponti to make two films back to back in Rome: this one and Blood for Dracula, which reused many of the same sets and stars.
Filming began March 20, 1973, at Cinecittà in Rome with an Italian crew. Production designer Enrico Job built the lab and castle.
Star Udo Kier (Baron Frankenstein) couldn't improvise, so director Paul Morrissey wrote the dialogue day by day, dictating it to Pat Hackett at his studio.
Joe Dallesandro (Nicholas) told Film Comment he had a falling-out with director Paul Morrissey on this shoot and wouldn't work unless lines were written for him: "I wouldn't talk."
The gore was an early job for Carlo Rambaldi, who later built E.T. in E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982). Antonio Margheriti shot the "breathing lungs" made from pigs' lungs.
Some Italian prints credit Antonio Margheriti as director under the name "Anthony M. Dawson." Udo Kier says Margheriti never directed the actors; the credit helped the film qualify as Italian.
Joe Dallesandro (Nicholas) is the "Little Joe" in Lou Reed's "Walk on the Wild Side." Reed saw Dallesandro in Flesh (1968) and wrote the third verse about him.
Monique van Vooren (Baroness Katrin) once suggested that a dancer in her nightclub act, Ronnie Walken, change his first name to Christopher. He did.
Swedish grindcore band Nasum took its name from a line in this film. Its song "Blind World" also samples the movie's dialogue.
Director Nicolas Winding Refn (Drive) has said this is the only film made by someone else that he wishes he'd directed.
Rated X by the MPAA for explicit sex and violence. The New York Times called it a "coy binge in degradation" and ran the headline "Butchery Binge."
The Italian dub, reworked with screenwriter Tonino Guerra to be funnier, renamed the Baron's children Systole and Diastole. In English they're Monica and Erik.
Joe Dallesandro (Nicholas) reportedly lost a Godfather screen test for Michael Corleone: Andy Warhol told Francis Ford Coppola's people he was a drug addict.
Joe Dallesandro, who plays farmhand Nicholas, spends roughly half the movie naked, according to Mondo Esoterica's review. The film made him and Udo Kier European cult stars.
Monique van Vooren (Baroness Katrin) also played the Penguin's associate on the 1968 TV series Batman, and was a judge at the 1969 Miss Universe pageant.
Britain made it a "video nasty." Cut by about 8 minutes in 1973, it was denied a video certificate, got a trimmed release in 1996, and was finally passed uncut in March 2006.
Cattle Decapitation's death-metal album Homovore samples this film's dialogue in the song "Carnal Fecophelia Due to Prolonged Exposure to Methane."
Udo Kier got word of a nice remark from director Roman Polanski in Interview magazine's Nov. 1973 issue. Andy Warhol sent Kier a copy with every page signed.
The Bedlam Files notes the film's camp tone is helped by deliberately silly sound touches, like loud slurping on the soundtrack during a sex scene.
Producer Carlo Ponti won an Oscar for La Strada, produced Doctor Zhivago, and married Sophia Loren. Here he bankrolled one of Italy's goriest 3-D oddities.
Composer Claudio Gizzi's score includes an arrangement of Richard Wagner's Tannhäuser overture, titled "The Creature Sees the Light."
The Italian cut, retitled "Il mostro è in tavola, barone... Frankenstein," ran 89 minutes. The original version was banned in Italy, and film historian Roberto Curti called its box office "mediocre."
The Bedlam Files says this gory Frankenstein spoof went on to influence the 1991 Japanese film The Last Frankenstein.
Bruce G. Hallenbeck, in Comedy-Horror Films, wrote that you find yourself "convulsed with laughter during some of the goriest scenes ever filmed."
Director Paul Morrissey made Flesh (1968), which launched Joe Dallesandro as a star, for just $4,000. It sold over 3 million tickets in West Germany.
AllMovie's Craig Butler said Paul Morrissey skewers the very countercultural sex revolutionaries who were his fans, making a "very conservative critique of hippie culture."
Udo Kier, who played both the Baron here and Dracula in Blood for Dracula, got his horror-icon status from these two films. He died November 23, 2025.
The film was re-released in its original 3-D version during the short-lived early-1980s 3-D craze, as "Andy Warhol's Frankenstein."
In 2012 Time Out polled horror authors, directors, actors and critics. Flesh for Frankenstein placed number 98 on its top 100 horror films list.
Dalila Di Lazzaro, who plays the female monster, later appeared in Phenomena (1985). She was an Italian model before acting.
Germany's cut version lost over 11 minutes. The uncut film was on the BPjM index until September 2024, and in December 2024 it got a "not under 16" rating.
The Simpsons referenced the film in the episode Treehouse of Horror XVI (2005).
A 2022 restoration from Vinegar Syndrome and the American Genre Film Archive presents the film in 3-D, pushing organs toward the camera.
The film is Criterion Collection spine #27 on DVD and #288 on laserdisc, a rare cult-horror entry in that prestige line.
Udo Kier remembered that Antonio Margheriti "was on the set, he came to the studio from time to time, but he never directed the actors. Never!"
Rotten Tomatoes shows 88% of 17 critics' reviews positive. It was panned in 1974 but is now a cult classic.
